paper_title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction. Counting mugs across home, for example, requires searching multiple rooms, opening closed storage, and tracking objects across views to avoid double-counting  (Fig. 1)  . The agent must also choose views that reveal occluded targets and decide when the search is complete. Yet an agent may report the correct count without observing every mug or checking every room. It may also make incorrect spatial judgments after collecting the required observations. Outcome correctness must therefore be evaluated alongside the tasks required observations and interactions. Existing benchmarks address different parts of this process. VSI-Bench [29] and MMSI-Bench [31] evaluate spatial question answering from preselected videos or images. EmbodiedQA [4] and OpenEQA [16] shift information gathering to the agent through question-driven navigation. EXPRESS-Bench [12] assesses answer grounding in the final observed image, while ESI-Bench [8] evaluates perception, locomotion, and manipulation for spatial QA. EmbodiedBench [30] and BEHAVIOR-Spatial [2] evaluate embodied tasks and spatial skills. Across these settings, final scores do not consistently distinguish correct outcomes from completed observation and interaction requirements. 1 Fig. 1 ROAM-Bench checks task outcomes and required observations and interactions. Counting mugs across home requires searching multiple rooms, checking rooms without mugs, and opening cupboard to find hidden mug. Independent checks verify the final count, target observations, room coverage, and container inspection. To address this gap, we introduce ROAM-Bench, which evaluates task outcomes together with the observations and interactions required to reach them. The benchmark comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups: grounding, aggregation, geometry, reference-frame integration, and goal-directed spatial action. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and separately verify required observations, search coverage, ordered interactions, geometry, and object placement. This verification helps distinguish missing observations from mistakes made after collecting them for deeper failure analysis. Task success requires these conditions together with correct outcome, measuring how exploration, spatial judgment, and action work together. Our platform, built on Isaac Sim [17], provides 27 furnished indoor environments generated with SceneSmith [19] and manually corrected for benchmark use. vision-language model (VLM) chooses predefined navigation and interaction skills, including moving, observing, opening, picking, and placing. The simulator executes these atomic skills under declared motion and interaction constraints. After each skill, the agent receives new view and action feedback before choosing its next step. The feedback reports collisions and object-handling outcomes, which the agent can use to adjust its plan. Our contributions are (1) comprehensive benchmark and evaluation protocol for embodied spatial intelligence, connecting exploration, spatial judgment, and goal-directed action. (2) An executable exploration platform with atomic actions, leveraging simulation oracles to verify task outcomes and taskrequired evidence. (3) Human and frontier VLM evaluations with supporting diagnostics covering information acquisition, precision, relocation failures, input sensitivity, and costs that include failures.

sections.title: 3.1 Task Taxonomy and Interaction
sections.content: To evaluate embodied active spatial intelligence, we design tasks that combine exploration, spatial reasoning, and interaction in different ways. For example, counting may require searching several rooms, gap measurement requires observing both edges, and relocation requires finding and moving the correct object. On our platform based on Isaac Sim [17], the agent gathers observations and interacts with objects until it completes the task. We then check the final result and whether the task is carried out as required. We group the 11 task types by their main answer or action  (Fig. 2)  . G1, semantic-spatial grounding, 3 Fig. 2 The 11 task types in five groups, illustrated with recorded camera observations, detail insets, and schematic annotations. Instructions are abbreviated. Relocation shows the target, destination, and placed-object stages of one episode. identifies objects and rooms. G2, spatial aggregation, counts objects or rooms across views. G3, metric and comparative geometry, estimates distances, areas, and gaps or compares proximity. G4, referenceframe integration, judges directions from reference objects or the agents final position and heading. G5, goal-directed spatial action, finds and transfers the specified object to its destination. Tasks describe targets through reference images of objects or surfaces, category names, and room names. To find named room, the agent must infer its function from the layout and furnishings. The instructions also guide exploration and spatial judgment: counting questions specify where to search, while direction questions specify the position and orientation from which directions are judged. The agent therefore needs to interpret the task before deciding where to look and what to observe. Atomic actions. All groups allow navigationmove, strafe, turn, look and object interactionopen, close, pick, place. G1, G2, and G5 also permit navigation to an object or ground point selected in the latest image, emphasizing search and object handling. G3 and G4 require movement distances and directions to be specified, testing metric and reference-frame reasoning. To specify target objects and navigation locations without ambiguity, we use pixel selection in the latest camera image for object interaction and image-point navigation.

sections.title: 3.3 Task Generation and Validation
sections.content: We generate questions, reference answers, and goal conditions from the objects, room assignments, and geometry recorded in each scene. We check task feasibility through an oracle trajectory generated using simulator state and the available skills. We then manually inspect the scene to verify the instructions, answers or goals, and observation and interaction checks described below. This includes checking which objects and rooms must be counted, how directions are defined, and which object must be picked and subsequently placed at which destination.

sections.title: 3.4.1 Agent Interaction
sections.content: At each round, the agent receives the task, reference images, latest camera image, available sensor readings, and feedback from its actions. Earlier observations and visualization of the traveled path help it relate the current view to previous locations. Before executing skill or submitting an answer or completion report, it can retrieve relevant earlier images using their text summaries. Retrieved images are added to the current round. Executing skill produces the next observation and action feedback. Actions that select image points refer to the latest camera image. Once the agent finishes, the evaluator checks the final result and whether the task is carried out as required  (Fig. 3)  .

Room options provide names, requiring models to infer room functions from layouts and furnishings. For GPT-6.1-sol and GPT-6-astra, room-function inference remains harder than local object recognition after passes. This contrast highlights the need to connect visible objects with rooms overall layout and function. Counting remains difficult after and pass. Counting errors persist for these models after both and pass. Completing observation checks does not ensure consistent global count, highlighting cross-view instance identity and quantity integration as demands of spatial reasoning. Free-space width is precision bottleneck. Gap width has the most models with median error above tolerance  (Fig. 5)  . Halving tolerances preserves the overall A/T ranking (Appendix E.3). Continuous errors reveal precision differences that binary scores can obscure. Task-defined frames challenge direction judgments. Across all seven models, relative-direction errors exceed path-integration errors after passes. These questions require constructing frame from two reference objects to locate third. Explicit representations of the frames origin and forward axis may help these judgments.

Correct pickup is the largest relocation bottleneck. All seven models lose the most episodes before
picking the correct object on the same relocation tasks. Later failures involve transferring that same object
and verifying destination support (see the relocation milestones in Table S11). This shared pattern identifies
target selection and correct pickup as the main relocation bottleneck.
sections.content: Target selection and correction dominate early failures. Wrong-object pickup dominates early failures in every model. Feedback can also explain why pick fails: the selected image point is on floor or wall, or the arm cannot reach the object. Some models select another point or move the base but repeat the same error. These failures highlight the need to verify target identity and use feedback to correct subsequent actions.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: ROAM-Bench evaluates exploration, spatial judgment, and goal-directed action through independent outcome and evidence checks. Human evaluators demonstrate successful task completion through the public observation and action interface. VLMs exhibit both correct outcomes with unmet task requirements and errors after stronger corroboration passes. Spatial-estimation and relocation failures further identify difficulties in grounding judgments and selecting the intended object. These findings motivate coherent cross-view instance representations, calibrated spatial judgment, and feedback-guided planning.

Task type and scene are associated with 0.466 and 0.197 of the observed between-task accuracy variance (η2), respectively. Their additive fit has in-sample R2 = 0.545. The associations overlap because tasks share both type and scene. We hold out each of the 27 scenes in turn and estimate task-type means from the remaining scenes. These means reduce squared prediction error by 41.46% relative to the training-mean baseline, showing that task type helps predict difficulty across the benchmark environments. sections.content: We compare recovering task-relevant observations from each models own exploration trajectory with supplying target observations beyond that trajectory. sections.title: I GT Trajectory and Spatial Sensors
sections.content: I.1 GT Trajectory Inputs GT trajectory judgment replaces exploration context with generated GT trajectory observations, retaining the task question and public reference images. Models answer without further exploration. The set contains the same 139 active-exploration tasks used for the historical-image comparisons. The 36 counting and room-comparison questions use 16 distinct scene RGB observations. These cover all task targets and include at least two background views. Remaining views are chosen by deterministic scene sampling without fixed quota per target. The 17 container-contents questions use 40 slots, applying the same view-selection rule to all public options. The other 86 questions use 12 slots. We construct GT trajectory observations from scene geometry and task-target annotations, then provide annotation-free RGB views. We check that the observations cover the task targets. Frame IDs do not indicate target identity or selection roles, and the views are presented in shuffled order. The model is told that views can repeat objects and must be matched to unique instances. Model-visible materials contain the task, public references, and scene observations. Target masks, instance counts, and correctness labels remain in private selection and scoring records. I.2 Spatial Sensor Inputs The sensor condition keeps the generated GT trajectory RGB observations and their order identical. It adds aligned radial-depth samples, camera positions, forward directions, and camera calibration. Radial depth measures distance from the camera in meters. The camera uses Z-up convention with equal horizontal and vertical focal lengths. These readings supply metric scale and coordinates across views.
